answers.answer: Embedded means the database engine runs in the application's process: code calls SQLite directly to execute SQL, with no separate database-server or network-query boundary. A persistent database uses a local file; in-memory operation is also available. Tables, joins, indexes and transactions remain supported. An application-local dataset fits direct local access and fewer services. Many application servers updating shared data across a network raise shared-access, coordination and synchronization needs, while each database still has only one writer. Client/server storage is often the better fit; SQLite can sit behind an application server using local storage. User count and size alone do not describe locality, competing writes, transaction duration or query work, so do not decide the choice. Separate device files do not automatically synchronize: additional software and conflict handling are needed.

evidence.quote: The engine runs inside your application's process. Your code calls SQLite directly, rather than sending queries to a separate database server.
A persistent database lives in a local file. SQLite also supports in-memory databases.
SQLite stores data in tables and supports SQL queries, joins, indexes, and transactions.
Often a better fit when many machines need shared database access or competing writes cannot take turns.
Measure write contention and transaction duration, not just the number of users.
Sharing changes between independent device or server copies requires additional software. Local transactions do not resolve conflicting edits elsewhere.

answers.answer: Affinity guides conversions in ordinary tables; a value has its own storage class, and an integer-declared column can retain unconvertible text. STRICT requires values to fit declared types after permitted conversions, except ANY columns. Primary keys identify rows, UNIQUE restricts duplicates, NOT NULL rejects missing values and CHECK rejects false conditions. Required values need NOT NULL because CHECK alone does not reject all missing values; foreign-key references may also be null unless forbidden. Foreign keys constrain references to existing rows. Before a transaction, enable PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on every connection and query PRAGMA foreign_keys to verify 1. A transaction groups database changes: commit accepts them and rollback cancels them. Atomicity means all changes succeed together or none take effect; consistency preserves defined rules; isolation controls concurrent visibility/write coordination and normally hides incomplete changes; durability preserves commits according to configured guarantees. Constraints define the rules and correct transaction logic is still needed for races and coordination. Rollback journaling records original data for undoing interrupted changes; durability settings that delay flushing can lose recent commits on power loss, and protection depends on reliable locking and storage honoring flush requests. External network effects are outside the database transaction and are not undone by rollback. Exact journaling or durability configuration choices are not supplied.

evidence.quote: Ordinary tables use affinity to guide conversions; each value has a storage class, such as integer, text or null. A declared integer column can retain text that cannot be converted.
Values must fit the declared type after permitted conversions, except columns explicitly declared ANY.
Primary keys identify rows; UNIQUE restricts duplicates, NOT NULL rejects missing values and CHECK rejects false conditions. Combine CHECK with NOT NULL when a missing value must also be invalid.

Constrain references to existing rows; null references are allowed unless separately forbidden. Before starting a transaction, enable enforcement on each connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, then query PRAGMA foreign_keys and check that it returns 1.
All changes succeed together, or none take effect.
Changes preserve the rules you defined.
Normal settings hide incomplete changes, but do not remove application races, lock waits or the need for correct transaction logic.
Committed changes survive failures according to the configured guarantees. This also requires reliable filesystem locking and storage that honors requests to flush data to persistent media.
Settings that delay flushing committed changes to persistent storage can lose recent transactions after a power failure.
Only database work inside the transaction is covered. Rollback does not reverse an external network side effect.
Records original data so SQLite can undo an interrupted change.

answers.answer: Several connections, even from different processes on one machine, may be active but only one may actively write each database at a time. Write contention is competing work trying to obtain that limited write access. SQLITE_BUSY means required access could not be obtained. Short write transactions reduce how long other writes wait; avoid waiting for network work inside one. A busy timeout or bounded retry can absorb brief contention, but failed attempts must be handled and some failures require retrying the transaction. These measures only wait or try again: they neither add a writer nor guarantee success. Rollback journaling records original data for undo and readers/writers can block one another. WAL records changes in a separate log, letting readers use stable snapshots while one writer commits. A checkpoint transfers logged changes into the main file. Long reads can delay checkpoint progress, allowing the WAL to grow. WAL remains single-writer and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine. The file/host must support reliable filesystem locking; the lesson does not supply a detailed shared-file or network-filesystem configuration procedure.

evidence.quote: SQLite supports multiple connections, including connections from different processes on the same machine. But each database allows only one active writer at a time.

A connection can receive this result when it cannot obtain required access. A busy timeout or bounded retry can tolerate brief contention; some failures require retrying the transaction. Waiting does not create another writer or guarantee success.
Keep write transactions short. A transaction that waits on a network request can hold up unrelated writes.
Records original data so SQLite can undo an interrupted change. In this mode, readers and writers can block each other.
Records changes in a separate log. Readers can continue using a stable snapshot while a writer commits changes.
Transfers logged changes into the main database file. Long-running reads can delay checkpoint progress and allow the log to grow.
WAL still allows only one writer, and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine.
This also requires reliable filesystem locking and storage that honors requests to flush data to persistent media.

answers.answer: An index is an additional access structure that can avoid scanning or sorting all rows. A query plan is the planner's chosen access and processing steps for filtering, joins, sorting and aggregation. For owner filtering and time ordering, a candidate inferred from the lesson is a composite index ordered by owner then time; match the actual filters and requested ordering, inspect EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for the chosen access/sort steps and measure representative queries. The lesson does not give an exact SQL definition, direction, output interpretation or guarantee that this candidate wins. Scans can be preferable for small tables or broad queries. Indexes consume space and require write maintenance; local queries still cost CPU, storage I/O and memory. The application/host still manages file permissions, capacity and recovery. Coordinate schema migrations with application versions and active access; some require table rebuilding and copying. Retain appropriate backups and test restoration and application usability. During active WAL operation, committed state may remain in the log, so copying the main file alone can omit required data. A supported consistent backup method addresses consistency. A verified quiescent copy would need assurance that the copied state contains all required committed data and cannot change during copying; the lesson does not teach a procedure to establish that state, so it does not justify assuming stopped writes alone make a main-file copy safe. Having a file proves neither consistency nor recovery time or successful usable restoration.

evidence.quote: Chooses access and processing steps for joins, filtering, sorting and aggregation. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows those steps.
An additional structure that can avoid scanning or sorting all rows. Match columns and their order to actual filters and requested ordering; a composite index contains multiple columns.
A scan can be preferable for small tables or broad queries. The planner need not use an index merely because it exists. Measure representative queries.
Local execution still uses CPU, storage I/O and memory. Indexes take space and add write maintenance; avoiding a network call does not make expensive work free.
The application and host still own filesystem permissions, storage capacity and recovery; embedded execution does not remove those responsibilities.
A migration changes stored structure. Coordinate it with application versions and active access; some changes require rebuilding a table and copying data.
Use a supported consistent backup method for an active database. Committed data may still be in the WAL, so copying only the main file can omit required state.
Manage access permissions and free space. Retain backups according to recovery needs, then test restoration and application usability. A backup file alone does not prove consistency or recovery time.

answers.answer: For one host with short occasional writes, SQLite is a plausible choice: direct local calls and files reduce service management, and the writers can plausibly take turns. Verify that contention and duration are acceptable; WAL can improve overlap with readers while keeping one writer. Several servers sustaining concurrent writes to shared data are a stronger client/server case: competing writes may not tolerate taking turns, and SQLite WAL is not a cross-machine shared-access solution. For either choice, define constraints and typing requirements, verify per-connection foreign-key enforcement, inspect and measure representative query plans and indexes, and arrange consistent backups plus restore tests. Before deciding, establish where data lives and which hosts/processes need access; measure competing write demand, busy failures/waiting, transaction duration, representative query cost, long-reader duration and WAL growth/checkpoint progress. These measurements are inferred from the lesson's stated mechanisms, not supplied benchmarks. Verify acceptable waiting/failure behavior, synchronization/conflict requirements, data rules, durability configuration and storage behavior, storage/free-space needs, migration coordination, and recovery needs with usable restore timing. No numeric workload threshold or benchmark outcome is supplied, so the recommendation remains conditional on those checks.

evidence.quote: The key questions are where the data lives and how much work competes to write it.
Direct local access, fewer services to run, and a database that can travel with the application.
Measure write contention and transaction duration, not just the number of users.
Often a better fit when many machines need shared database access or competing writes cannot take turns. SQLite can still be suitable behind an application server with local storage.
WAL still allows only one writer, and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine.
Long-running reads can delay checkpoint progress and allow the log to grow.
Measure representative queries.
Retain backups according to recovery needs, then test restoration and application usability.
